1303.title: the seasons
1303.hook: Krishna names spring as his season of flowers; Charaka's spring is also a thaw
1303.howItsDone: People who follow Ayurveda eat lighter in spring, avoid daytime sleep and move more, as the classical texts advise, and Hindu communities in parts of India mark the season with Vasant Panchami and Holi.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the seasons and Charaka's winter: a strong inner fire held in by the cold, fed with warm, substantial food.

Of the seasons, the one that brings flowers. That's Krishna in the Bhagavad Gita, paraphrased, in a chapter where he names, kind after kind, where his glory shows: among rivers, among mountains, among months. And among the seasons, he chooses spring. So in the Gita, spring arrives already crowned: blossom, color, the year waking up. But Ayurveda's classical texts read the same season with a second eye, and what they see isn't only flowers. It's a thaw. Today, spring, both ways.
screen: `OF SEASONS, THE ONE THAT BRINGS FLOWERS.` → `SPRING, ALREADY CROWNED.` → `A SECOND EYE: A THAW.`

segments.voice: The Gita's word is kusumakara, the flower-bringer: spring as poetry and as worship. Charaka's chapter on the seasons calls spring vasanta, and its reading, paraphrased, goes like this. Through the winter, kapha builds up in the body, the heavy, cool, steady quality. Then the spring sun melts it, the way sun melts snow, and the melting stirs things up. The digestive fire that was so strong in winter is dampened. People feel heavy, slow, congested. So the advice turns. Avoid foods that are heavy, sour, sweet and rich. Don't sleep through the day. Move: exercise, a brisk rub of the skin. Eat lighter grains. And, nicely, spend time in gardens and woods, where spring is doing its flowering. Hold the two readings side by side. First, one season, two pictures, and both are true. The tree blossoms; the yard is mud. A text of devotion sees the first; a text of health insists on the second. Second, the advice reverses yesterday's. What winter asked for, spring asks you to lay down. The seasons don't hand out one diet for the year. Third, the festival calendar runs alongside. In parts of India, spring brings Vasant Panchami, when Saraswati is honored, and Holi, with colors thrown in the open air. Out of the house, into the light, moving. The thaw and the blossom, together.
screen: `KUSUMAKARA, A STOREHOUSE OF FLOWERS` · `WINTER'S KAPHA MELTS` · `LIGHTER FOOD, MORE MOVEMENT` · `ONE SEASON, TWO PICTURES`

segments.voice: Sit tall, as if a thread drew you up from the crown of the head, and notice any heaviness in the shoulders, the jaw, the eyelids. Let three exhales run a little longer than the inhales, and on each one let a heavy place soften, the way snow goes soft in the sun. If you pray, hold one flower in mind, offered.
The seasons. In spring, two readings together: the Gita's season of flowers, and Charaka's thaw that asks for lighter food and more movement. Today's word.
Your line: the seasons. Spring lays down what winter asked you to carry. See you tomorrow.

1304.title: the seasons
1304.hook: a clay pot of water by a gate on a hot afternoon: Charaka's summer is about putting back what the sun takes
1304.howItsDone: People who follow Ayurveda keep summer cool and slow, as the classical texts describe: sweet, cool, liquid food and drink, less hard exercise, and rest in the heat; in parts of India households set out water for passersby and birds in the hot months.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the seasons in spring: the Gita's season of flowers, and Charaka's thaw that asks for lighter food and more movement.

A hot afternoon on the plains of north India. Shutters pulled, the street outside nearly empty. By a gate, on a little stand, sits a clay pot, its sides dark and damp, with a steel cup beside it for anyone walking past. Nobody guards it. Nobody charges for it. The pot sweats, and the water inside stays cool. It's a plain picture of summer, and it holds much of Charaka's summer advice in one object. Today, the hot season.
screen: `A HOT AFTERNOON. SHUTTERS PULLED.` → `A CLAY POT BY THE GATE.` → `TODAY, THE HOT SEASON.`

segments.voice: Charaka's chapter on the seasons calls summer grishma. His picture, paraphrased: the sun's strong rays draw the moisture out of the world, and out of the body along with it. So the answer is to put back what the sun takes. Food and drink that are sweet, cool and liquid, with a little richness: rice, milk, cooling drinks. Go easy on salty, sour, sharp and hot things, and on hard exercise in the heat. Then a small surprise. Elsewhere Charaka is wary of sleeping in the daytime. In summer, he allows it. The nights are short and the days are heavy, so the afternoon rest is part of the cure. Cool rooms, too, and moonlight in the evening. Three things to see. First, the logic we've followed all along: meet a quality with its opposite. Dry and hot is answered with moist and cool. Second, it's a season for doing less. Not pushing through: slowing down and sheltering. Third, back to the pot by the gate. Ayurveda's summer says replace what the heat takes from you. The household habit stretches that to whoever walks by. In parts of India, people set out water in the hot months for strangers, and a shallow dish for birds. Charaka's summer, turned outward: the opposite of the heat, offered to anyone thirsty.
screen: `GRISHMA: THE SUN TAKES` · `PUT THE MOISTURE BACK` · `THE ONE SEASON FOR A NAP` · `A POT OF WATER BY THE GATE`

The seasons. In summer, Charaka's reading is a sun that draws out moisture, answered with sweet, cool, liquid food, rest and shade. Today's word.
Your line: the seasons. What the heat takes, a cup of water gives back. Same time tomorrow.

1305.title: the seasons
1305.hook: the first rain brings a craving for fried snacks; Charaka says the body's fire is at its lowest
1305.howItsDone: People who follow Ayurveda eat lightly in the rainy season, drink boiled water and keep dry, as the classical texts advise; some Hindus keep a vow during Chaturmas, the sacred stretch of the rainy months.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the seasons in summer: the sun draws the moisture out, so you put it back, and maybe set a cup out for someone else.

The first rain on dry ground has a smell, and it often arrives to cheering. Kids run out into it. Somebody puts a pan of oil on the stove, and within the hour there are pakoras, hot and crisp, and cups of sweet tea, and everyone at the window watching the street turn into a river. A real pleasure. And the old Ayurvedic text has a gentle, slightly inconvenient note about it. Today, the rains.
screen: `THE FIRST RAIN ON DRY GROUND.` → `PAKORAS AT THE WINDOW.` → `A GENTLE, INCONVENIENT NOTE.`

segments.voice: Charaka calls the rainy season varsha. His reading, paraphrased: the body comes into the rains already worn down by the hot months, and then the rain weakens the digestive fire further. The air is damp, the ground gives off vapor, the water is muddied, and the body's qualities are stirred up all at once. So just as the pakoras are frying, the text says your fire is burning low. Its advice: light food, grains kept from an earlier harvest, water boiled or collected clean, a little honey. Go easy on heavy meals, hard exertion and daytime sleep. Keep dry, wear clean, fragrant clothes, and don't wade about in the wet. Notice what the text does and doesn't say. First, the pleasure isn't scolded. The rains aren't bad; the body is tender in them, and asks for care. Second, it's a season for staying in. Travel is hard, the roads wash out, the body is weak. Third, Hindu practice has its own staying-in. Tradition calls a stretch of the rainy months Chaturmas. Some people keep a vow then, giving something up for the season, and wandering renunciants, tradition says, stop wandering and stay in one place until the rains end. Some say Vishnu himself sleeps through these months. A god resting, monks staying put, an old physician advising light food and dry feet: different texts, the same season. Slow down, stay close, wait it out.
screen: `VARSHA: THE RAINS ARRIVE` · `THE FIRE BURNS LOW` · `LIGHT FOOD, CLEAN WATER, DRY FEET` · `CHATURMAS: STAYING PUT`

segments.voice: Decide that for the next while you won't go anywhere, not even in your head to the next thing, and let sounds come and go like rain on a roof. Each time the mind wanders off, bring it home, gently, to the breath. If you pray, say a name of God once, and rest in it.
The seasons. In the rains, Charaka's reading is a weak inner fire and a tender body, answered with light food, clean water and staying close. Today's word.

1306.title: the seasons
1306.hook: water warmed by the sun all day and cooled by the moon all night: Charaka's autumn has a name for it
1306.howItsDone: People who follow Ayurveda cool the body in autumn with bitter and sweet foods and ghee, as the classical texts advise, and on Sharad Purnima some Hindu families leave rice cooked in milk under the full moon overnight.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the seasons in the rains: a low inner fire, light food, dry feet, and the monks who stay put.

Swan water. All day the autumn sun warms it. All night the moon shines on it and it cools. Charaka's chapter on the seasons calls water like that hamsodaka, and says, paraphrased, that such water, made clean by time and the stars, is like nectar. Plain water, left out in the open, as a small calendar of the sky. On our last day with the seasons, the year comes round to autumn.
screen: `WARMED BY THE SUN, COOLED BY THE MOON.` → `HAMSODAKA, SWAN WATER.` → `THE YEAR COMES ROUND TO AUTUMN.`

segments.voice: Charaka calls autumn sharad, and his reading, paraphrased, starts with a jolt. Through the rains the body grew used to cool and damp. Then the clouds clear, the sun comes out hard, and the body is suddenly heated. Pitta, the hot, sharp quality, built up quietly in the rains, flares. So the advice is cooling: sweet, bitter and astringent foods, light meals, ghee prepared with bitter herbs. Avoid too much sun, curds, heavy food and daytime sleep. And then the gentle part: swan water to drink, and moonlight in the early part of the night. Three last things. First, a season isn't just its weather. It's the weather after the last one. The same sun means something different after months of rain. Second, the moon. Hindu practice gives autumn a full moon of its own, Sharad Purnima, and in some homes a pot of rice and milk is left out under it overnight, then eaten in the morning: cooling food, cooled by the moon, in the very season Charaka asks for both. Third, the whole year at once. Charaka's chapter names six seasons: two winters, then spring, summer, the rains and autumn. One move runs through every one: notice what the season brings, and answer it with its opposite. The fire held in by cold, fed. The thaw, lightened. The heat, cooled with water. The rains, met with care. And autumn's sudden sun, cooled with bitter things and moonlight.
screen: `SHARAD: SUDDEN SUN AFTER RAIN` · `COOL WHAT THE RAINS STORED UP` · `RICE AND MILK UNDER THE MOON` · `SIX SEASONS, ONE MOVE`

1307.title: food as practice
1307.hook: a young man asks his father what Brahman is, and the first answer he finds is food
1307.howItsDone: In Hindu homes that keep these customs, food is offered before it is eaten, and complaining about food or wasting it is avoided, a stance the Taittiriya Upanishad puts as a vow not to speak ill of food.

segments.voice: Yesterday closed the seasons: Charaka's year, every season answered with its opposite, ending in swan water and moonlight.

A son goes to his father with one request. Teach me Brahman, he says: the ultimate reality, the ground of everything. His name is Bhrigu. His father is Varuna. And Varuna doesn't lecture. He gives a riddle and sends him away to work it out. Bhrigu goes off, sits with it, practices, and comes back with an answer that might seem almost too ordinary for the question. He says: food. A run of days on food as practice starts with that answer.
screen: `TEACH ME BRAHMAN.` → `A RIDDLE, NOT A LECTURE.` → `THE FIRST ANSWER: FOOD.`

segments.voice: The story is in the Taittiriya Upanishad. Varuna's riddle, paraphrased: that from which beings are born, by which, once born, they live, and into which they return, seek to know that. That is Brahman. And one instruction: seek it through tapas, disciplined, inward effort. So Bhrigu does, and he comes to see, the text says, that food is Brahman. From food beings are born. By food they live. Into food they return. It fits every line of the riddle. Now the twist. Varuna doesn't say, well done, you're finished. He gives the same instruction again, seek it through tapas, and sends him out once more. Step by step Bhrigu goes deeper: to breath, to mind, to understanding, and at last to bliss. Three things. First, food isn't thrown away when he goes deeper. It's the first floor of the house, and the house stands on it. Second, the Upanishad draws vows out of it. Do not speak ill of food. Do not despise food. Make much food. Not diet rules but a stance: food handled with respect, because it was the first thing Bhrigu found holy. Third, the Ayurvedic texts arrive somewhere close from another direction. Charaka treats food as what sustains the life of living beings, the ground health is built on, which is why these days give food a whole week. So food as practice doesn't start with a rule about what to eat. It starts with seeing what food is.
screen: `BHRIGU ASKS HIS FATHER` · `FOOD IS BRAHMAN` · `SEARCH AGAIN, AND GO DEEPER` · `DO NOT SPEAK ILL OF FOOD`

Go slowly, as far back as you can, and let it become a long line of things you didn't make. If you pray, give thanks for one link in that line.

1308.title: food as practice
1308.hook: halfway through a good plate, the body says enough; Charaka and the Gita both have a word for that moment
1308.howItsDone: People who follow Ayurveda eat in measure, the amount their digestion handles well, and leave some room in the stomach rather than eating until full, as the classical texts advise.

segments.voice: Yesterday, food as practice began with Bhrigu, who searched for Brahman and first found food, and his vow: do not speak ill of food.

Halfway through a plate of something really good, there's a moment. The food still tastes wonderful. Nothing has gone wrong. But under the pleasure, the body has quietly said: that's about right. It's a small signal, easy to sail straight past, especially with a few bites left and nobody watching. The old texts noticed that moment and gave it a word. The Charaka Samhita opens its chapter on the daily round with it, and the Bhagavad Gita makes it a condition for yoga. Today, the measure.
screen: `HALFWAY THROUGH A GOOD PLATE.` → `THE BODY SAYS: ABOUT RIGHT.` → `TODAY, THE MEASURE.`

segments.voice: The word is matra, measure. Charaka's chapter on the daily round begins, paraphrased: one should eat in measure. And the measure isn't a fixed number for everyone. It depends on the strength of a person's digestive fire. The right amount is the amount digested well and in good time, without trouble. Your measure is yours. Elsewhere Charaka gives a picture that's easy to keep. Divide the stomach's room into three parts: one for solid food, one for drink, and one left for the body's own movements, the doshas, to work in. Paraphrased, but the picture really is that simple: don't fill it to the top. The Bhagavad Gita comes at the same moment from the side of practice. Krishna says, paraphrased, that yoga is not for the one who eats too much, nor for the one who doesn't eat at all. It's for the one who is measured in eating, in sleeping and waking, in work and rest. For that person, he says, yoga becomes the end of sorrow. Put the two together. First, both reject the extremes: not stuffing, and not starving. Second, measure isn't a rule handed down from outside. It's a listening, a matter of knowing your own fire. Third, it's a practice you get to try at every meal, so it's never far away. The moment halfway through the plate is the whole lesson. The skill is hearing it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, food as practice meant measure, matra: the amount your own fire digests well, with room left over.

A phone propped against a water glass. A video playing. A fork going up and down more or less on its own, and at some point the plate is empty and it's hard to say what was on it. That's an ordinary lunch now, and nobody needs a lecture about it. But set it beside a passage in the Charaka Samhita that lays out how to eat. Not what. How. Read today, it sounds startlingly current. Today, the way of eating.
screen: `A PHONE AGAINST A WATER GLASS.` → `NOT WHAT TO EAT. HOW.` → `TODAY, THE WAY OF EATING.`

segments.voice: In its section on how food should be taken, Charaka gives a set of guidelines. Paraphrased: eat food that is warm. Eat in measure, yesterday's word. Eat after the last meal has been digested, not on top of it. Eat in a pleasant place, with what you need at hand. Eat neither too fast nor too slowly. Don't talk or laugh through the meal. Eat with your mind on the food, knowing what suits you. What stands out? First, almost none of this is about ingredients. It's about attention, pace and place. The same plate eaten in a rush while scrolling, or slowly at a table, is in this view not quite the same meal. Second, the rules aren't harsh. A pleasant place is one of them; the text wants you comfortable. Third, the week behind us has been building to this. Each season changed what to eat. Bhrigu showed that food is worth reverence. Measure said how much. And today Charaka says how. Here the Ayurvedic lens meets household practice. In some Hindu homes, before the first bite, someone says a verse from the fourth chapter of the Bhagavad Gita: the offering is Brahman, the food offered is Brahman, offered by Brahman into the fire that is Brahman. With words or without, the pause itself does what Charaka asks. It puts the mind on the food before the hand moves.

segments.voice: If there's water or tea near you, pick it up, feel its weight and its warmth or cool, and take one sip, holding it a moment before you follow it down; if nothing's at hand, do the same with a breath. Then set the cup down and sit with whatever is left: the taste, the warmth, the quiet. If you pray, say a line of grace your family uses.
Food as practice. Charaka's way of eating: warm food, after the last meal is digested, in a pleasant place, at an easy pace, with the mind on the food. Today's word.
